lessons.name: Analyze passages from The Great Gatsby : Part 1

pieces.text: Read the following passage from

. In this excerpt, the narrator, Nick Carraway, is attending one of Jay Gatsby's extravagant parties for the first time. Nick is sitting at a table with Jordan Baker, the only person he knows at the party, and having a conversation with a stranger.

textContent.text: I turned again to my new acquaintance. "This is an unusual party for me. I haven't even seen the host. I live over there—" I waved my hand at the invisible hedge in the distance, "and this man Gatsby sent over his chauffeur with an invitation."
For a moment he looked at me as if he failed to understand.
"I'm Gatsby," he said suddenly.
"What!" I exclaimed. "Oh, I beg your pardon."
"I thought you knew, old sport. I'm afraid I'm not a very good host."

pieces.text: He smiled understandingly—much more than understandingly. It was one of those rare smiles with a quality of eternal reassurance in it, that you may come across four or five times in life. It faced—or seemed to face—the whole eternal world for an instant, and then concentrated on

with an irresistible prejudice in your favour. It understood you just so far as you wanted to be understood, believed in you as you would like to believe in yourself, and assured you that it had precisely the impression of you that, at your best, you hoped to convey. Precisely at that point it vanished—and I was looking at an elegant young roughneck, a year or two over thirty, whose elaborate formality of speech just missed being absurd. Some time before he introduced himself I'd got a strong impression that he was picking his words with care.

textContent.text: Almost at the moment when Mr. Gatsby identified himself a butler hurried toward him with the information that Chicago was calling him on the wire. He excused himself with a small bow that included each of us in turn.
"If you want anything just ask for it, old sport," he urged me. "Excuse me. I will rejoin you later."
When he was gone I turned immediately to Jordan—constrained to assure her of my surprise. I had expected that Mr. Gatsby would be a florid and corpulent person in his middle years.
"Who is he?" I demanded. "Do you know?"
"He's just a man named Gatsby."
"Where is he from, I mean? And what does he do?"

pieces.text: "Now
started on the subject," she answered with a wan smile. "Well, he told me once he was an Oxford man."

textContent.text: A dim background started to take shape behind him, but at her next remark it faded away.
"However, I don't believe it."
"Why not?"
"I don't know," she insisted, "I just don't think he went there."

Something in her tone reminded me of the other girl's "I think he killed a man," and had the effect of stimulating my curiosity. I would have accepted without question the information that Gatsby sprang from the swamps of Louisiana or from the lower East Side of New York. That was comprehensible. But young men didn't—at least in my provincial inexperience I believed they didn't—drift coolly out of nowhere and buy a palace on Long Island Sound.
"Anyhow, he gives large parties," said Jordan, changing the subject with an urban distaste for the concrete. "And I like large parties. They're so intimate. At small parties there isn't any privacy."
<citation>Adapted from F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby</citation>

content.text: Based on the passage, which of the following is most likely true about Gatsby?

choices.text: He consciously presents himself in a way that emphasizes his position in upper-class society.
He is embarrassed by his poor hosting skills and uses work as an excuse to escape.
He is comfortable being rude because he thinks he is more important than his guests.
He lacks interest in forming personal connections with unfamiliar guests at his party.

pieces.text: Narrated by Nick Carraway, an observant outsider to the extravagance of upper-class society in the 1920s,
tells the tragic story of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious self-made millionaire who goes to extraordinary lengths to rewrite his personal history and shape his destiny.

textContent.text: When Nick moves from the Midwest to Long Island, he becomes mesmerized by rumors swirling around his next-door neighbor, Jay Gatsby, who throws enormous, glittering parties at his palatial estate.
Nick is pulled into the drama surrounding Gatsby's obsession with Daisy Buchanan, as well as the salacious affair between Daisy's husband Tom and a woman from Queens named Myrtle Wilson.

pieces.text: Set in New York City during the "Jazz Age," a term popularized by the novel's author,
is a sobering account of greed, wealth inequality, and moral collapse set to the tempo of jazz music, fast cars, and easy money.

contents.text: The details in this passage support this inference about Gatsby:

text.text: He consciously presents himself in a way that emphasizes his position in upper-class society.

contents.text: These inferences are not well supported in the passage:

text.text: He is embarrassed by his poor hosting skills and uses work as an excuse to escape.

content.text: Though Gatsby owns up to not being a very good host, he doesn't seem to be embarrassed about being aloof and disengaged at his own party. He is called away for work during the conversation with Nick, but nothing in the passage suggests that he is using work as an excuse to remove himself from the table.

text.text: He is comfortable being rude because he thinks he is more important than his guests.

content.text: Gatsby apologizes for not being a good host and politely excuses himself when he has to leave, suggesting that he does not like to be rude to his guests.

text.text: He lacks interest in forming personal connections with unfamiliar guests at his party.

content.text: Gatsby engages Nick in a conversation and displays a warm and welcoming smile. This shows that Gatsby has an interest in forming a personal connection with Nick and the other guests.

contents.text: The details in these quotes suggest that Gatsby consciously presents himself in a way that emphasizes his position in upper-class society:

text.text: "This is an unusual party for me. I haven't even seen the host. I live over there—" I waved my hand at the invisible hedge in the distance, "and this man Gatsby sent over his chauffeur with an invitation."

content.text: This act of sending a chauffeur instead of a simple invitation card or message highlights Gatsby's desire to impress and assert his social standing, showcasing a deliberate effort to stand out and affirm his place among the social elite.

text.text: Precisely at that point it vanished—and I was looking at an elegant young roughneck, a year or two over thirty, whose elaborate formality of speech just missed being absurd. Some time before he introduced himself I'd got a strong impression that he was picking his words with care.

content.text: Gatsby carefully selects his words and speaks in a way that is so formal it is almost comical, suggesting a deliberate effort to present himself in a refined manner. This implies that he is conscious of his image and wants to portray himself as a member of the upper class.

tells the tragic story of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious self-made millionaire who goes to extraordinary lengths to rewrite his personal history and shape his destiny.

textContent.text: When Nick moves from the Midwest to Long Island, he becomes mesmerized by rumors swirling around his next-door neighbor, Jay Gatsby, who throws enormous, glittering parties at his palatial estate.
Nick is pulled into the drama surrounding Gatsby's obsession with Daisy Buchanan, as well as the salacious affair between Daisy's husband Tom and a woman from Queens named Myrtle Wilson.

is a sobering account of greed, wealth inequality, and moral collapse set to the tempo of jazz music, fast cars, and easy money.

content.text: Though Gatsby owns up to not being a very good host, he doesn't seem to be embarrassed about being aloof and disengaged at his own party. content.text: Gatsby apologizes for not being a good host and politely excuses himself when he has to leave, suggesting that he does not like to be rude to his guests.

contents.text: The phrase "elegant young roughneck" presents a paradox. The term "elegant" suggests Gatsby's sophistication and refined demeanor, which are essential to his social standing. text.text: Gatsby projects a close friendship with guests, but he is actually distant and secretive.

content.text: Despite Gatsby's personal invitations and the fact that he calls Nick "old sport," his actual interaction with guests is limited and mysterious, and his guests are left guessing at his background. This suggests that while Gatsby gives the impression of being a friendly and accessible host, he maintains distance and an air of secrecy.

contents.text: These inferences are not well supported in the passage:

text.text: Gatsby pretends to like everyone but privately despises and mistrusts them.

content.text: The passage does not provide any evidence that Gatsby is distrustful or insincere in his attempts to be friendly and polite.

text.text: Gatsby enjoys company, but he is more comfortable working than hosting.

content.text: While Gatsby is called away for a work obligation, the passage does not indicate that he has a preference for working over entertaining.

text.text: Gatsby creates an atmosphere of openness by sharing personal stories with his guests.

content.text: The passage portrays Gatsby as secretive about his past, not as open. He does not share any personal stories.

pieces.text: Narrated by Nick Carraway, an observant outsider to the extravagance of upper-class society in the 1920s,
tells the tragic story of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious self-made millionaire who goes to extraordinary lengths to rewrite his personal history and shape his destiny.

textContent.text: When Nick moves from the Midwest to Long Island, he becomes mesmerized by rumors swirling around his next-door neighbor, Jay Gatsby, who throws enormous, glittering parties at his palatial estate.
Nick is pulled into the drama surrounding Gatsby's obsession with Daisy Buchanan, as well as the salacious affair between Daisy's husband Tom and a woman from Queens named Myrtle Wilson.

pieces.text: Set in New York City during the "Jazz Age," a term popularized by the novel's author,
is a sobering account of greed, wealth inequality, and moral collapse set to the tempo of jazz music, fast cars, and easy money.

content.text: Though Gatsby owns up to not being a very good host, he doesn't seem to be embarrassed about being aloof and disengaged at his own party. content.text: Gatsby engages Nick in a conversation and displays a warm and welcoming smile. This shows that Gatsby has an interest in forming a personal connection with Nick and the other guests.

text.text: He is comfortable being rude because he thinks he is more important than his guests.

content.text: Gatsby apologizes for not being a good host and politely excuses himself when he has to leave, suggesting that he does not like to be rude to his guests.

elements.text: directly supports the claim;

explanationText.text: This evidence directly supports the claim, comes from a credible source, and is not anecdotal.

text.text: U.S. census figures indicate that the rate of marriage is at an all-time low.

explanationText.text: This evidence does not directly support the claim. It gives a fact about marriage in general, but it does not focus on any particular generation.

explanationText.text: This evidence is not credible. Anyone can make a post on a social network. It's also anecdotal, since it shows the perspective of only one person.

lessons.name: Commas with direct addresses, introductory elements, absolute phrases, interjections, interrupters, and antithetical phrases

header.text: Correct the text by inserting or removing commas. There should be a total of one comma.

sentences.text: <u>Mild interjections and introductory words</u>
Use a comma after mild interjections, as well as words like yes, no, well, and however, when they are followed by a complete sentence.
Oh, the sunset is so beautiful.
Yes, that sounds great!
<u>Introductory phrases</u>

Use a comma after most introductory phrases—such as participle phrases, infinitive phrases, and long prepositional phrases—when they are followed by a complete sentence. (Commas are not usually necessary after short prepositional phrases of one or two words.)
In just a few weeks, Mr. Chen will be leaving for his trip to France.
Breathing heavily, Maddie sprinted the last few meters of the race.
<u>Absolute phrases</u>
Use commas to set off absolute phrases. An absolute phrase usually consists of a noun followed by a participle phrase, adjective phrase, or other modifier.
Hands shaking, Tony opened the letter and read it aloud.
Amanda rushed inside the house, her clothes already wet from the rain.
<u>Direct addresses</u>
Use commas to set off the name of a person being spoken to.
Bella, thank you.
Thank you, Bella, for your help.
<u>Interrupters</u>
Use commas to set off interrupters, which are words, phrases, or clauses that interrupt the sentence with extra, or parenthetical, information.
You, of course, may have a different opinion.
The new theme park won't open, I'm sorry to say, until next year.
<u>Antithetical phrases</u>
Use commas to set off phrases that use the words not or unlike to qualify adjacent text.
Alexander the Great was Macedonian, not Greek.
Tara, unlike Megan, finds chemistry fascinating.

sentences.text: <u>Mild interjections and introductory words</u>
Use a comma after mild interjections, as well as words like yes, no, well, and however, when they are followed by a complete sentence.
Oh, the sunset is so beautiful.
Yes, that sounds great!
<u>Introductory phrases</u>

Use a comma after most introductory phrases—such as participle phrases, infinitive phrases, and long prepositional phrases—when they are followed by a complete sentence. (Commas are not usually necessary after short prepositional phrases of one or two words.)
In just a few weeks, Mr. Chen will be leaving for his trip to France.
Breathing heavily, Maddie sprinted the last few meters of the race.
<u>Absolute phrases</u>
Use commas to set off absolute phrases. An absolute phrase usually consists of a noun followed by a participle phrase, adjective phrase, or other modifier.
Hands shaking, Tony opened the letter and read it aloud.
Amanda rushed inside the house, her clothes already wet from the rain.
<u>Direct addresses</u>
Use commas to set off the name of a person being spoken to.
Bella, thank you.
Thank you, Bella, for your help.
<u>Interrupters</u>
Use commas to set off interrupters, which are words, phrases, or clauses that interrupt the sentence with extra, or parenthetical, information.
You, of course, may have a different opinion.
The new theme park won't open, I'm sorry to say, until next year.
<u>Antithetical phrases</u>
Use commas to set off phrases that use the words not or unlike to qualify adjacent text.
Alexander the Great was Macedonian, not Greek.
Tara, unlike Megan, finds chemistry fascinating.
